reponse:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Acting on observation differences to cancel episode-constant offsets
PROPOSAL: An additive offset that stays fixed for a whole episode cancels exactly in the difference between two consecutive observations, so we train a policy whose inputs are the last eight observation differences and the last eight actions rather than the raw state. We use TD3+BC and IQL on the D4RL Hopper, Walker2d, HalfCheetah and AntMaze-medium datasets, rewriting every stored transition into difference form before training, with a gated recurrent encoder to recover velocity-like and phase-like information that the absolute state would otherwise carry. At test time each episode receives a per-dimension offset taken from real series: electricity-load, exchange-rate and sensor-drift records rescaled to twice the per-dimension standard deviation of the dataset. We report normalised return over two hundred ordered episodes and the fraction of the clean-observation return retained.
CONTROLS: The same algorithms on raw observations, the same algorithms with Gaussian-noise augmentation, a policy given the true offset, the difference policy with the action inputs removed, and all methods on zero-offset episodes to measure what the loss of absolute position costs on AntMaze.
COST: 320
PREDICTION: The difference policy should retain most of its clean return on locomotion tasks, where the offset dominates the failure of raw-state policies, and lose a visible part on AntMaze, where absolute position matters for reaching the goal. If the Gaussian-augmented baselines match it, episode-constant offsets are no harder than noise and the premise of this plan is wrong.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Estimating the episode offset from dynamics consistency during the episode
PROPOSAL: We learn an ensemble of forward dynamics models on the offline dataset and, at deployment, treat the unknown per-dimension offset as a parameter to be estimated from the transitions observed so far in the episode. After each step we solve a small least-squares problem that finds the offset vector under which the corrected transitions best agree with the learned dynamics, warm-started from the previous estimate, and we feed the corrected observation to a frozen IQL policy. Before the first estimate is available the policy acts on an offset-free guess. We evaluate on D4RL locomotion tasks and on Adroit pen and door manipulation, with offsets drawn from recorded calibration logs and from piecewise-constant jumps, and we report the return and the estimation error as a function of the step index within the episode.
CONTROLS: The frozen policy on uncorrected observations, the same policy given the exact offset, a Kalman filter that assumes Gaussian drift in the offset, the estimator run with a single dynamics model instead of the ensemble, and the estimator fed transitions from a different episode to check that it uses the current episode rather than a dataset prior.
COST: 260
PREDICTION: Estimation error should fall below the policy's tolerance within the first dozen steps on locomotion tasks, so that returns approach the exact-offset reference. On manipulation tasks whose dynamics barely move in early steps the estimate may stay ambiguous for longer and returns may remain closer to the uncorrected policy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Offset randomisation with a recurrent behaviour-regularised actor
PROPOSAL: We train a recurrent actor-critic with behaviour-cloning regularisation on standard offline locomotion and manipulation datasets, applying to every sampled trajectory a per-dimension additive offset held constant along the whole trajectory. Offsets come from a broad mixture of uniform, heavy-tailed and sparse vectors in which only a few dimensions move, so that the recurrent state learns to recognise the current offset from its first transitions rather than memorise one family of shifts. At test time we evaluate on an ordered stream of episodes whose offsets follow real series that never appear during training, including exchange-rate records and stepwise sensor recalibration logs, and we report normalised return along the stream together with the recurrent state's offset-decoding accuracy from a linear probe.
CONTROLS: The same recurrent actor trained without any offset, a feed-forward actor trained with the same offsets, the feed-forward actor on clean observations as an upper reference, and a variant in which training offsets are drawn from the same series family as the test stream, to measure how much is gained by matching the family.
COST: 450
PREDICTION: The recurrent actor trained on the broad mixture should recover most of the clean return within a handful of steps per episode and generalise to unseen series without retraining. Should the family-matched variant clearly dominate, the mixture is too narrow and the approach depends on knowing the pattern in advance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A benchmark of episodic observation offsets drawn from real series
PROPOSAL: We build an evaluation suite in which a policy trained on a standard offline dataset is tested on an ordered stream of episodes, each with a per-dimension additive offset taken from recorded real-world series: electricity demand, currency rates, industrial sensor drift and scheduled recalibration logs, each rescaled to a chosen multiple of the dimension's standard deviation. The suite covers Datasets for Deep Data-Driven Reinforcement Learning (D4RL) locomotion and maze tasks and Adroit manipulation. We run implicit Q-learning (IQL), conservative Q-learning (CQL), twin delayed deep deterministic policy gradient with behaviour cloning (TD3+BC), decision transformer (DT) and the robust offline reinforcement learning method RORL, and we add two variants of each that receive, respectively, the past offsets of the previous ten episodes and no past information at all. We report normalised return over the stream, the within-episode return curve, and the gap to each method's clean score.
CONTROLS: Every method on clean observations, every method under independent Gaussian noise of equal magnitude, a random policy, and the stream replayed with the same offsets in shuffled order to tell apart temporal structure from marginal magnitude.
COST: 180
PREDICTION: Methods trained for noise should lose most of their return under episode-constant offsets even at magnitudes where noise is harmless, and access to past offsets should help only on series with slow drift. If shuffled order changes nothing, temporal structure carries no exploitable information at these horizons.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Pessimistic action selection over a posterior of offset hypotheses
PROPOSAL: We keep, during each test episode, a discrete set of candidate offset vectors per dimension on a grid centred on zero, and a weight for each candidate updated after every step from how well the corrected transition agrees with an ensemble of dynamics models learned offline. Actions are chosen to maximise the expected value of a frozen Q-function under the current weights minus a penalty on the spread of that value across candidates, which makes the agent cautious while the offset is still ambiguous and increasingly decisive as the weights concentrate. The Q-function and dynamics models are trained with conservative Q-learning on publicly released offline locomotion and manipulation datasets. Test streams use offsets following recorded series of sensor drift and abrupt recalibration steps, and we report return along the stream and the entropy of the candidate weights over the episode.
CONTROLS: The same Q-function acting on uncorrected observations, acting with the true offset, acting with the weighted mean candidate and no spread penalty, the weights frozen at uniform throughout the episode, and a finer and a coarser grid of candidates.
COST: 300
PREDICTION: The spread penalty should matter mainly in the first steps of each episode, after which the weighted-mean variant catches up. On tasks where early actions are irreversible, such as falling in Hopper, the penalty should give a clear gain over the weighted mean.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Optimising a latent offset code at test time without touching the weights
PROPOSAL: We train a policy and a dynamics model that both take, besides the observation, a low-dimensional code vector; during offline training the code is produced by an encoder from the true offset applied to the trajectory, and the offsets are sampled from a wide synthetic family. At deployment the encoder is discarded and the code is treated as a free variable: at each step we take a few gradient steps on the code to minimise the dynamics model's prediction error over the transitions seen in the episode so far, keeping all network weights frozen. The policy then acts with the updated code. We test on D4RL locomotion and AntMaze datasets with test offsets from real series of calibration drift and sudden jumps, reporting return along an ordered stream of episodes and the cosine similarity between the inferred code and the one the discarded encoder would have produced.
CONTROLS: The policy with the code fixed at the training mean, the policy with the code from the true offset, the code optimised on transitions drawn from a different episode, and a baseline that fine-tunes all weights on the same transitions.
COST: 280
PREDICTION: The inferred code should approach the encoder's code within the first steps and recover most of the return of the true-offset variant. If optimising on another episode's transitions works as well, the code is not capturing the offset and the gain comes from something else.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Using a short history of past offsets as a prior for in-episode inference
PROPOSAL: We study the deployment variant in which the agent receives the offsets of a limited number of past episodes at discrete intervals, and we ask how much that history is worth once combined with in-episode inference. We fit a nonparametric prior over offsets, a kernel density on the last twenty recorded offsets per dimension, and use it to initialise a particle set that is then reweighted during the episode from the agreement of corrected transitions with a learned dynamics ensemble. The policy, trained with TD3+BC on D4RL Walker2d, HalfCheetah and Adroit relocate datasets, acts on the particle-weighted corrected observation. We evaluate on streams whose offsets follow three kinds of real series, slow drift, periodic recalibration and irregular jumps, and we report return against the number of past offsets provided, from none to twenty.
CONTROLS: Particles initialised uniformly without any history, the prior used alone without in-episode reweighting, a direct forecaster trained on the past offsets and used without correction, and the policy given the exact offset.
COST: 240
PREDICTION: History should help on slow drift and matter little on irregular jumps, where in-episode reweighting should carry the result. We expect the prior-only variant to fail on jumps, which would show that forecasting past offsets cannot replace inference from the current episode.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Shift-invariant state encoders learned by trajectory-level contrast
PROPOSAL: We pretrain an encoder on the offline dataset with a contrastive objective in which two views of the same trajectory segment differ only by a per-dimension additive constant sampled anew for each view, while segments from different trajectories or with different actions are negatives. The encoder is thus pushed to represent the segment through quantities that an episode-constant shift leaves unchanged, such as velocities, contact timing and action-conditioned changes, and we then train an IQL policy on the frozen encoder output of a window of the last ten observations. Evaluation uses D4RL locomotion, AntMaze and Adroit datasets with test-time offsets from recorded sensor-drift and recalibration series applied per episode, and we measure return along the stream as well as a linear probe of how much offset information survives in the embedding.
CONTROLS: IQL on raw observations, IQL on the same window with an encoder trained without the shift augmentation, an encoder trained with Gaussian-noise views instead of constant shifts, and the policy given offset-free observations as an upper reference.
COST: 350
PREDICTION: The shift-contrastive encoder should keep most of its clean return on locomotion while the noise-view encoder should not, and the probe should recover almost no offset. On AntMaze the loss of absolute position may cost part of the return, which would mark the limit of pure invariance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Identifiability conditions for an episode-constant observation offset
PROPOSAL: We give a formal account of identifiability for the test-time setting with additive offsets. With a known deterministic transition function, the offset is identified after k steps exactly when the stacked Jacobians of the corrected transition residuals with respect to the offset have full column rank, and we derive the minimal k for linear systems and for systems whose dynamics are locally affine. We then bound the return lost by a plug-in policy, one that acts on the current estimate, as the sum of a term that decays with the identification time and a term proportional to the dynamics model's error, and we show that extrapolation from past offsets can only lower the first term. Numerically we verify the rank condition on learned dynamics models of D4RL Hopper, Walker2d and AntMaze datasets, counting the number of steps until the condition holds along test episodes with offsets taken from recorded series.
CONTROLS: Linear systems with analytically known identification time, randomly initialised dynamics models of the same architecture, and models trained on half of the dataset to measure how model error moves the bound.
COST: 40
PREDICTION: The rank condition should hold within a few steps on locomotion tasks and take longer on AntMaze, where several dimensions barely move early in an episode. The bound should be loose but ordered correctly across tasks; if the empirical loss does not follow the predicted ordering, the model-error term is dominating.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Set-membership planning under offsets consistent with the episode so far
PROPOSAL: We combine a learned dynamics ensemble with model-predictive planning in which the unknown offset is not estimated to a point but kept as a set: after each step, the set of offsets consistent with every transition seen so far is tightened using the ensemble's disagreement as the error bound on each residual, giving a box per dimension. The planner samples action sequences, evaluates each on the corners and the centre of the current box with a frozen TD3+BC value function as terminal reward, and executes the first action of the sequence with the best worst-case return. We run the method on D4RL HalfCheetah, Hopper and AntMaze-umaze datasets and on Adroit door, with test offsets from recorded series of recalibration jumps and slow drift, reporting return along an ordered stream and the box width over steps.
CONTROLS: The same planner with the box replaced by its centre point, the planner on uncorrected observations, the planner with the true offset, and the planner with the ensemble disagreement replaced by a fixed error bound.
COST: 520
PREDICTION: Worst-case planning should pay off early in the episode and converge to the centre-point planner as the box shrinks. If the fixed-bound variant performs equally, the ensemble disagreement is not what makes the set tight enough to matter.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Offset-aware recurrent policy for offline navigation with drifting sensors
PROPOSAL: Train a behaviour-regularised actor on Maze2d and AntMaze datasets from D4RL after corrupting every stored trajectory with an additive observation offset drawn once per episode, while a recurrent encoder learns to infer that offset from the opening observation-action pairs and passes it to the actor. At deployment, replay 30 offset streams made of step changes, sinusoids, stochastic walks and recorded sensor drift that never occur in training, and track normalised return by episode index, with special attention to the first ten steps of every episode.
CONTROLS: Compare against a behaviour-regularised policy trained on clean data only and evaluated under the same offset streams. Compare against the same actor handed the true offset at each step. Compare with and without the encoder output, with the rest of the network held the same. Compare across stream types that were absent from training, using the same encoder weights.
COST: 240
PREDICTION: The encoder should recover most of the return lost to offsets within the first ten steps, with the largest gains on abrupt streams. The approach is falsified when the gap to the true-offset actor stays large on streams unlike those seen in training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Offset-robust actor with ensemble critics for offline manipulation under calibration drift
PROPOSAL: Fit a behaviour-regularised actor on FrankaKitchen and Adroit datasets from D4RL, perturbing stored trajectories with an additive per-joint offset drawn once per episode, while an ensemble of critics trained with pessimistic penalties supplies value estimates that damp the effect of mismatched states. At deployment, replay 30 offset streams made of step changes, sinusoids, stochastic walks and recorded calibration drift that never occur in training, and track success rate by episode index, with special attention to the first ten steps of every episode.
CONTROLS: Compare against a behaviour-regularised policy trained on a different dataset family and evaluated on clean observations. Compare against the same actor handed the true reward at each step. Compare with and without the critic ensemble, with the rest of the network held the same. Compare across dataset qualities that were present in training, using the same ensemble weights.
COST: 240
PREDICTION: The critic ensemble should keep success close to its clean level in the first ten steps, with the largest gains on abrupt streams. The approach is falsified when the drop under offsets stays large on streams unlike those seen in training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Sliding-window offset estimator trained from corrupted offline trajectories
PROPOSAL: Learn a transformer that maps the last 20 observation-action pairs to a latent offset code, trained on HalfCheetah and Hopper medium-replay data from D4RL where each trajectory carries a synthetic offset that stays constant inside an episode and changes between episodes, then condition a CQL policy on that code. Test on 25 offset series drawn from sawtooth calibration patterns, abrupt regime switches and non-Markovian bursts that were not used for training, and measure return in the first quarter of each episode separately from the rest.
CONTROLS: Compare against a CQL policy with the same architecture trained on uncorrupted trajectories and tested on the same series. Compare short, medium and long windows while the series are held the same. Compare with the code replaced by codes taken from other episodes, using identical weights otherwise. Compare across offset magnitudes that go beyond the training range.
COST: 620
PREDICTION: Return in the first quarter of an episode should rise clearly over the uncorrupted-data policy, with medium windows doing best on bursts. The idea is in trouble when codes from other episodes score close to the true codes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Latent offset codes from attention over short histories in offline locomotion
PROPOSAL: Train an attention encoder that reads the last 20 observation-action pairs and emits a latent offset code, using Walker2d and Ant medium-expert data from D4RL in which every trajectory is shifted by a synthetic offset that stays constant inside an episode and changes between episodes, and feed the code to a CQL policy. Evaluate on 25 offset series made of drifting calibration ramps, abrupt regime switches and non-Markovian bursts absent from training, and measure return in the first quarter of each episode separately from the rest.
CONTROLS: Compare against a CQL policy with the same architecture trained on a larger share of the trajectories and tested on the same series. Compare narrow, medium and wide attention layers while the series are held the same. Compare with layer normalisation removed from the encoder, using identical weights otherwise. Compare across data subsamples that stay within the training amount.
COST: 620
PREDICTION: Return in the first quarter of an episode should rise clearly over the narrower policy, with medium attention layers doing best on bursts. The idea is in trouble when the removed normalisation leaves scores close to the full encoder.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Test-time offset recovery from model consistency in offline walking tasks
PROPOSAL: Pretrain a world model on the D4RL walker2d medium-expert data, then at deployment estimate the episode offset by finding the shift under which a few opening observations best agree with the model's one-step predictions, and feed the recovered shift to a pretrained IQL policy. Use 40 offset series including long stable stretches, sudden jumps and non-Markovian patterns, with the first 15 steps of each episode used for estimation and the remaining steps used for control, and score per-episode normalised return together with offset recovery error.
CONTROLS: Compare against the IQL policy acting on raw shifted observations in the same episodes. Compare against the same policy given the true offset from the first step. Compare the estimation step run on the first 15 steps versus on the last 15 steps, both with the same model. Compare across jump magnitudes that cover the whole range met at deployment, including the largest.
COST: 1100
PREDICTION: Recovered shifts should track the true ones within the first 15 steps and lift return over the raw-observation policy on large jumps. The method is refuted by streams where early recovery error stays high and return stays near the raw-observation level.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Dynamics-agreement search for episode-wide shifts in offline hopper control
PROPOSAL: Fit a probabilistic dynamics ensemble to D4RL hopper medium-replay trajectories, then in each deployment episode choose the shift that maximises the likelihood of the opening transitions under the ensemble and pass the chosen shift to an IQL policy trained beforehand. Run 40 offset series with slow ramps, sudden jumps and non-Markovian bursts, using 15 opening steps for the search and the later steps for control, and score normalised return per episode together with the shift estimation gap.
CONTROLS: Compare against the IQL policy acting on raw unshifted observations in the same episodes. Compare against the same policy given the true action from the first step. Compare the search step run on the first 15 steps versus on the first 25 steps, both with the same ensemble. Compare across jump magnitudes that cover only the smallest part of the range met at deployment.
COST: 1100
PREDICTION: Estimated shifts should land near the true ones within the opening steps and lift return over the unshifted-observation policy on mid-sized jumps. The method is refuted by streams where the estimation gap stays high and return stays near the unshifted level.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Per-joint offset recovery for robot arm manipulation from offline demonstrations
PROPOSAL: Train a variational history encoder on Adroit pen and door human-demonstration data plus cloned trajectories, corrupting each episode with an additive per-joint offset that differs across episodes, and condition a BC-regularised actor on the encoder's posterior mean. At deployment, stream 20 offset series with abrupt switches and slow drift, and for each episode measure task success rate, tracking it separately for the first 10 steps and the remainder, and also record the encoder posterior error.
CONTROLS: Measure success rate for the actor given raw shifted observations on the same series. Measure success rate for the actor given the true offset. Measure success rate with and without the posterior input, using identical weights otherwise. Measure success rate on series from patterns unseen during training.
COST: 70
PREDICTION: Success should recover most of the clean level in the opening 10 steps, with drift series easier than switches. The approach is falsified when success on unseen patterns sits close to the raw-observation actor.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: History encoding of joint shifts for door and hammer manipulation from offline data
PROPOSAL: Fit a recurrent variational encoder to Adroit hammer and relocate demonstrations together with expert rollouts, shifting each trajectory by a per-joint additive offset that varies between episodes, and give the encoder's latent mean as extra input to a BC-regularised actor. During deployment, run 20 offset series that combine abrupt switches with slow drift, and for every episode score how well the encoder reconstructs its inputs, split into the first 10 steps and the rest, alongside the actor's imitation loss.
CONTROLS: Measure imitation loss for the actor given raw shifted observations on the same series. Measure imitation loss for the actor given the true offset. Measure imitation loss with and without the latent input, using identical weights otherwise. Measure imitation loss on series from patterns seen during training.
COST: 70
PREDICTION: Reconstruction should improve markedly in the opening 10 steps, with drift series easier than switches. The approach is falsified when imitation loss on seen patterns sits close to the raw-observation actor.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Forecast-free offset estimation for offline policies when past offsets are absent
PROPOSAL: Train a policy on D4RL antmaze-umaze and antmaze-medium diverse data under offsets resampled each episode, using a belief module that is updated from the observation stream alone and exposes a latent state estimate to a behaviour-regularised actor. Evaluate on 30 test streams with step changes, bursts and slowly varying offsets, in two deployments: one where the agent never sees earlier offsets, and one where it receives sparse records of them, and measure success rate from the very first step of each episode.
CONTROLS: Compare against a forecaster that extrapolates the next offset from the past records. Compare against the same actor with a recurrent filter over raw observations. Compare with and without the belief module in the deployment lacking records. Compare across stream types where extrapolation is easy and where it is hard.
COST: 380
PREDICTION: The belief module should reach a success rate near the record-using forecaster on slow streams and clearly higher on bursts. The idea is refuted by bursts where the filter over raw observations scores the same as the belief module.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Belief tracking of observation shifts in offline kitchen and block-stacking tasks
PROPOSAL: Fit a policy on kitchen-partial and kitchen-mixed trajectories from D4RL, resampling the shift for every episode, with a belief tracker fed only by incoming observations that hands a latent estimate to an IQL actor. Test on 30 streams mixing step changes, bursts and gentle ramps under two deployments, one without any record of earlier shifts and one with sparse logs, and count completed subtasks beginning at step zero of every episode.
CONTROLS: Compare against a forecaster that extrapolates the next observation from the past logs. Compare against the same actor with a recurrent filter over clean observations. Compare with and without the belief module in the deployment with full logs. Compare across stream types where extrapolation is easy and where it is simple.
COST: 380
PREDICTION: The belief module should reach completed subtasks near the log-using forecaster on slow streams and clearly higher on bursts. The idea is refuted by bursts where the filter over clean observations scores the same as the belief module.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Shift-cancelling inputs for a sequence policy under episodic offsets
PROPOSAL: Because a shift that is constant within an episode disappears from the difference between successive observations, we train a decision transformer whose context holds the last twelve observation differences and actions in place of the raw states, on D4RL Hopper, Walker2d and AntMaze-medium datasets, with returns-to-go unchanged. A small learned module re-estimates the absolute position from the differences and the initial observation's distribution when a task needs it. Test streams apply per-episode offsets from recorded recalibration and drift series, and we report return along the stream and within each episode.
CONTROLS: The decision transformer on raw observations, the same model retrained with random-noise augmentation, the model given the true offset, the difference model without the position module, and offsets on half of the dimensions only, over three seeds.
COST: 380
PREDICTION: The difference model should keep most of its clean return on locomotion from the first step of every episode and lose part of it on AntMaze, where position matters. If the raw model with noise augmentation matches it, constant shifts are no harder than noise and this design is beside the point.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Forecasting the next episode's offset from the recorded offset history
PROPOSAL: We treat the sequence of past offsets as a multivariate time series and train a forecaster, a small temporal convolution network with a quantile head, on the offsets recorded during the first part of each deployment stream. Before each new episode the forecaster predicts the coming offset per dimension, the prediction is subtracted from every observation of that episode, and a frozen TD3+BC policy trained on D4RL Hopper, Walker2d and AntMaze-medium acts on the corrected observations. Streams follow recorded recalibration and drift series, and we report return along the stream together with the forecaster's error and its quantile coverage.
CONTROLS: A persistence forecast that repeats the last recorded offset of the stream, a seasonal-naive forecast, a zero forecast as placebo, a gradient-boosted forecaster on lagged features, the frozen policy on uncorrected observations, and the policy given the true offset, over three seeds.
COST: 380
PREDICTION: The learned forecaster should beat persistence on drifting series and give returns near the true-offset reference where the series are regular. On irregular jump series its error will be large and the corrected policy may fall below the uncorrected one.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Encoders made invariant to constant shifts by trajectory contrast
PROPOSAL: We pretrain a state encoder on the offline dataset with a contrastive loss whose positive pairs are two copies of the same trajectory window shifted by different per-dimension constants and whose negatives are windows from other trajectories, then train IQL on the frozen encoder output of the last ten observations and actions. The encoder is thereby pushed towards velocities, contacts and action effects that no episode-constant shift alters. Evaluation runs on D4RL locomotion and Adroit datasets with per-episode offsets from recorded recalibration logs and currency rates, reporting return along the stream and a linear probe of offset information left in the embedding.
CONTROLS: IQL on raw observations, IQL on the same window with an encoder trained without the shift views, an encoder trained with Gaussian-noise views, RORL as an external baseline checked against its published numbers on clean data, the policy on clean observations as the upper reference, and an evaluation under independent noise, over three seeds.
COST: 420
PREDICTION: The shift-contrastive encoder should keep most of the clean return where the noise-view encoder collapses, and the probe should recover almost no offset. If the noise-view encoder does as well, invariance to constant shifts is already obtained by noise training and the specific design adds nothing.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial observation perturbations during offline training for deployment reliability
PROPOSAL: We train IQL on D4RL locomotion and Adroit datasets while perturbing each sampled observation with a worst-case vector found by a few projected gradient steps inside a bounded ball, following the practice of test-time robust offline methods, and we regularise the critic to be smooth around perturbed states. The bound is set to the magnitude of the deployment shifts, and we select the ball radius on a held-out split of the dataset. We then evaluate on streams of episodes whose offsets follow recorded recalibration logs and currency rates, reporting return along the stream and the critic's smoothness on test states.
CONTROLS: IQL without perturbation, IQL with random perturbations of equal magnitude in place of adversarial ones, RORL as an external baseline, the perturbation bound at three settings, the policy on clean observations as the ceiling, and evaluation under independent Gaussian noise of the same magnitude, over three seeds.
COST: 420
PREDICTION: Adversarial training should give the largest gain under noise and a smaller one under constant shifts, where the perturbation seen in training is a per-step worst case rather than a persistent offset. If returns under shifts stay near the unperturbed baseline, smoothness alone does not help with systematic misalignment.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Particle inference of per-dimension offsets with a learned model
PROPOSAL: We run, inside every test episode, a particle filter over the offset vector whose particles are initialised from a wide heavy-tailed prior and reweighted at each step by the likelihood of the corrected transition under a dynamics ensemble trained offline, with resampling when the effective sample size drops. A frozen CQL policy acts on the observation corrected by the weighted particle mean. We evaluate on D4RL Hopper, HalfCheetah and AntMaze-umaze with offsets from recorded jump and drift series, reporting return along the stream and the error of the particle mean per step.
CONTROLS: The policy on uncorrected observations, the policy with the true offset, the filter with a Gaussian prior of small width, the filter driven by a randomly initialised dynamics model, and the particle count at three settings, over three seeds.
COST: 220
PREDICTION: The particle mean should converge within the first steps on locomotion and bring return near the true-offset variant from early in each episode. If the random-model filter does as well, the dynamics model is not what drives the correction.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Few-episode online adaptation of an offline policy to each new offset pattern
PROPOSAL: We fine-tune a CQL policy pretrained on D4RL Hopper, HalfCheetah and AntMaze-umaze whenever the deployment stream enters a new regime, using the first few episodes of that regime as online interaction data with a small learning rate and a behaviour-cloning anchor to the pretrained policy. Regime changes are detected from a drop in the running return, and the adapted policy is then used until the next detected change. Streams follow recorded jump and drift series, and we report return along the stream, the number of adaptation phases triggered and the return during adaptation episodes.
CONTROLS: The pretrained policy without adaptation as the floor, adaptation with the anchor removed, the learning rate at three settings, adaptation triggered at fixed intervals instead of by detection, and the policy given the true offset, over three seeds.
COST: 220
PREDICTION: Adaptation should lift return on long stable regimes and cost return during the first episodes of each regime. Where regimes change every episode, as in the jump series, there may be no phase in which the adapted policy is useful.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Identification time of an episode-constant offset and its return cost
PROPOSAL: We derive when the offset can be recovered from a known deterministic transition function: after k steps it is determined exactly when the stacked Jacobians of the corrected residuals with respect to the offset have full column rank, and we give the minimal k for linear and locally affine dynamics. We then bound the return lost by a plug-in policy acting on the current estimate by a term decaying with the identification time plus a term proportional to model error. Numerically we check the rank condition on dynamics models learned from D4RL Hopper and AntMaze datasets, counting steps until it holds on episodes with offsets from recorded series.
CONTROLS: Linear systems with known analytic identification time, randomly initialised models of the same architecture, and models trained on half the data to see how model error moves the bound.
COST: 60
PREDICTION: The condition should hold within a few steps on Hopper and later on AntMaze, where several dimensions barely move at first. If the empirical loss does not follow the predicted ordering across tasks, the model-error term dominates and the bound is uninformative.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Context-conditioned meta-learning across varying rewards and dynamics
PROPOSAL: We train a context-conditioned policy on a distribution of offline datasets in which the reward function and the transition dynamics vary across tasks, Hopper and AntMaze variants with altered body masses, friction coefficients and goal rewards, using a permutation-invariant context encoder over short transition windows and a conservative critic. At deployment the context is computed from the first transitions of each episode and the policy adapts its behaviour without any weight change. We evaluate on held-out combinations of mass, friction and reward and on streams in which these factors change every episode, reporting return along the stream and the context's accuracy at recovering the factors.
CONTROLS: A single policy trained on the pooled datasets without context, an oracle policy given the true factors, the context encoder fed windows from a different task shuffled across the batch, and training on half the task combinations.
COST: 60
PREDICTION: The context policy should beat the pooled policy on held-out combinations and approach the oracle. If the swapped-context variant performs as well, the policy is not using the context and the adaptation is illusory.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Worst-case planning over the offsets still consistent with the episode
PROPOSAL: We keep, during each test episode, a box of offsets per dimension that is tightened after every step to those values under which all corrected transitions so far are explained by a dynamics ensemble within its disagreement bound, and we plan with sampled action sequences evaluated at the box corners and centre, using a frozen TD3+BC critic as terminal value and executing the first action of the sequence with the best worst case. Experiments cover D4RL HalfCheetah, Hopper and Adroit door with offsets from recorded recalibration and drift series, reporting return along the stream and the box width per step.
CONTROLS: The planner at the box centre only, the planner on uncorrected observations, the planner with the true offset, a fixed error bound in place of the ensemble disagreement, and the critic acting alone without planning, over three seeds.
COST: 500
PREDICTION: Worst-case planning should help in the first steps of each episode and converge to the centre planner as the box shrinks, with the largest gain on Hopper where early mistakes end the episode. If the fixed-bound variant does equally well, ensemble disagreement is not what keeps the box useful.

TITLE: Learning rendering-invariant state encoders across block-structured observation functions
PROPOSAL: We render the D4RL HalfCheetah, Hopper and Adroit door datasets into pixel observations under several rendering functions, camera placements, textures and lighting, and train an encoder with a bisimulation objective so that two images produced from the same underlying state under different renderings map to the same code. A TD3+BC policy is trained on the encoder output. At deployment the agent faces renderings never seen in training, and we report return per rendering and the encoder's ability to recover the underlying state from a linear probe.
CONTROLS: A pixel policy trained on a single rendering, the policy on the true low-dimensional state, an encoder trained with reconstruction instead of bisimulation, a randomly initialised encoder as placebo, and training on half the renderings, over three seeds.
COST: 500
PREDICTION: The bisimulation encoder should generalise to unseen renderings far better than the single-rendering policy and approach the state policy. If the reconstruction encoder does as well, the invariance comes from data diversity rather than from the objective.
